clue.text: Close-up of a celebrity

definitions.meaning: in photography a close-up is a large, near shot of a subject
an important, famous person, a VIP or bigwig

explanation.definitionFit: A photographer's tight framing is a large shot, and an influential figure is informally called by the same phrase, so both senses share one expression.

clue.text: Sailing ship unladen? How bizarre!

annotationWithheld.why: Sailing ship unladen? How bizarre! — BARQUE with O (nothing) inside, but 'unladen' must both signal the insertion and supply the O, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Grotesque people scrambling royal eggs

indicators.note: eggs being scrambled suggests the letters of the phrase are mixed up into a new order

explanation.surface: Ugly people are making a mess of cooking the royal breakfast eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Carved monsters on church roofs are grotesque figures, and by extension the word is used for very ugly people.

clue.text: Board game of Neanderthal man

indicators.note: the game is made of letters taken from inside the phrase that follows, so the word signals a hidden run

explanation.surface: A board game supposedly played by prehistoric man.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of 'NeanderTHAL MAn'.
explanation.definitionFit: Halma is a strategy game played by moving pegs or pieces across a chequered board.

clue.text: Discoloured threads in weave

indicators.note: to weave is to interlace threads, so the letters of the words before it are worked into a new pattern

explanation.surface: Threads woven into a fabric have lost their colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weave' reworks the letters of THREADS and IN together.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal that is tarnished has dulled or lost its colour, so it is discoloured.

clue.text: Reading article out

indicators.note: out here means the letters are put out of place and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone reads a newspaper article out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a public performance such as a reading of poems or prose aloud.

clue.text: Power to keep gravity in check

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the word for a check holds the abbreviation for gravity

parts.note: a rein is a check or restraint
G is the physics symbol for gravity

explanation.surface: Authority is needed to keep weighty matters under control.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's period of rule is the time they hold sovereign power.

clue.text: People up here for river game

parts.note: the Cam is the river that flows through the university city
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: People come up here to enjoy a game on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: Students are said to 'go up' to an English university, so the definition describes the town people go up to.
explanation.definitionFit: British students speak of 'going up' to a university such as the one on the Cam, so it is a place people go up to.

clue.text: Memento of king in Eton, possibly

indicators.note: the letter for king is placed inside the rearranged letters
possibly means the word may be in another arrangement

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A keepsake of a king who was at Eton school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges ETON as TOEN, and 'in' puts K inside it. Eton is a famous English private school.
explanation.definitionFit: A token is a small object kept as a reminder, much like a souvenir.

clue.text: Conifers Charles ordered

indicators.note: putting letters in order means arranging them anew, so this name is rearranged

explanation.surface: Charles orders some cone-bearing trees for his garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Larch trees bear cones, so they are a kind of conifer, though unusual in shedding their needles.

clue.text: Larrup endlessly, perhaps, in the country

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the remaining letters may be arranged another way
without its end, so the last letter of the word is taken away

explanation.surface: Beating someone without stopping, perhaps out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the last letter P from LARRUP (to thrash), and 'perhaps' rearranges LARRU. 'Endlessly' looks like it means 'without pause'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rural describes things located in the countryside rather than towns.

clue.text: High powered employee of shower manufacturer

parts.note: a shower is a brief fall of rain
a maker is one who manufactures

explanation.surface: A top executive working for a company that makes showers.
explanation.walkthrough: In business slang the term is used for a high-earning executive who brings in lots of money.
explanation.definitionFit: Business slang for a star executive who brings in lots of revenue and clients.

clue.text: Cutting allowance? Not I, anyway!

parts.note: a quota is a fixed share or allowance

indicators.note: anyway suggests the letters can be put in any way, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to accept a reduced allowance for themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges NOTI as TION. 'Cutting' looks like a reduction but is a press cutting.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutting from a newspaper and a quoted passage are both extracts taken from a longer text.

clue.text: Organized church spread in North America

parts.note: to run an event is to organize it, so 'organized' gives the past tense

explanation.surface: An organized church spreads its influence across North America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organized' looks like an anagram signal but gives a synonym. A 'spread' is American slang for a large farm or estate.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage a spread is a large farm or cattle property.

clue.text: Conspicuous success of cycle in late traffic

indicators.note: the cycle's letter is placed inside the rearranged letters
traffic suggests movement and dealing, so the letters are shifted around

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cycle, as in c/s for cycles per second

explanation.surface: A cyclist making a striking success of riding through late traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'traffic' rearranges LATE as ELAT, and 'in' puts C inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Éclat, borrowed from French, means brilliant display or striking acclaim.

clue.text: Line often held to give someone a buzz?

definitions.text: Line often held to give someone a buzz?

parts.words: Line often held to give someone a buzz?
parts.note: a phone line is 'held' while waiting, and making a call is to give someone a buzz or ring

explanation.surface: A rope held tight to give someone a thrill.
explanation.definitionFit: A phone is the instrument for making calls, which people informally call buzzing someone.

clue.text: His Excellency concentrate on top gear?

parts.note: HE is the abbreviation for His Excellency, an ambassador's title
to address a problem is to concentrate on it

explanation.surface: An ambassador focuses on getting the very best equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top gear' looks like the highest speed but means clothing for the top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worn on the head, such as a hat or crown, is clothing for the top.

clue.text: Life protection for neck

definitions.meaning: life insurance, which British usage calls life ...
neck is cheek or nerve, boldness

explanation.definitionFit: Assurance is both cover against death in British insurance terms and self-confidence bordering on cheek.

clue.text: What Archie Rice tried to do — sign on as volunteer at home

definitions.text: What Archie Rice tried to do

parts.note: to enter a competition is to sign on for it
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force
in means at home

explanation.surface: A man signs up to be a volunteer soldier based at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Archie Rice is the music-hall performer in John Osborne's play The Entertainer.
explanation.definitionFit: Archie Rice is a fading stage comedian, whose job was to amuse an audience.

clue.text: Final pieces of plots used subtly

indicators.note: subtly suggests the letters are deviously rearranged

explanation.surface: The endings of stories use their plots in a subtle way.
explanation.definitionFit: Postludes are pieces of music played at the end, especially closing voluntaries in church.

clue.text: Lobs in sports grounds

definitions.meaning: fields where football or cricket is played

explanation.definitionFit: To throw a ball is to toss it, and the marked-out fields for football or cricket share the name.

clue.text: Class of chemical compounds from trees

indicators.note: from here means the letters are made from those of the next word, rearranged

explanation.surface: Chemicals that are extracted from trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Esters are organic compounds formed from an acid and an alcohol, often fragrant.

clue.text: Concerned with warnings, takes video back

parts.note: re means concerning or about
to get wind of something is to receive a warning hint

explanation.surface: Someone worried about warnings plays a video back.
explanation.definitionFit: Winding a tape back returns it to the start, as one does with a video cassette.

clue.text: Trek, carrying piano on streetcar

indicators.note: the vehicle carries the musical letter along at its rear

parts.note: a tram is a streetcar
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A long journey moving a piano on a streetcar.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk a long way heavily, a trek on foot.

clue.text: This lighting is bad!

parts.note: the lighting here is the criminal setting of a fire, which is bad in the moral sense

explanation.surface: A complaint about poor illumination.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is a crime, a wicked kind of fire-lighting.

clue.text: Restrain salary in spiral course

parts.note: to cork something is to stop it up or restrain it
screw is old British slang for wages

explanation.surface: Keeping wages down on a winding course.
explanation.definitionFit: A path that twists like the helix of a wine opener is spiral.

clue.text: Century not recorded when he led India?

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
a live broadcast is not recorded

explanation.surface: A hundred years unrecorded in the history of a ruler of India.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Clive led British forces in India in the 18th century.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Clive, 'Clive of India', commanded the East India Company's forces and governed Bengal.

clue.text: Archbishop of Canterbury

annotationWithheld.why: Archbishop of Canterbury (5) — appears cut short: LANG (Cosmo Lang) is an archbishop but nothing in the clue as held gives the S or a definition such as 'cant'

clue.text: Irish not a problem for this past master

indicators.note: a problem suggests something knotty, so the letters are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A scholar of the past finds Irish no difficulty at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'problem' rearranges the letters of IRISH and NOT A.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who studies and writes about past events is an expert on bygone times.

clue.text: Not for the first time, a profit

parts.note: a gain is a profit

explanation.surface: Making a profit, and not for the first time.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something once more means it is happening a further time.

clue.text: Frank seeing that about?

parts.note: since means because, seeing that
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A man named Frank, noticed hanging around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name but is the adjective meaning honest.
explanation.definitionFit: A frank person speaks honestly and genuinely.

clue.text: Trains with battering-rams

definitions.meaning: siege machines were once called ... of war

explanation.definitionFit: Locomotives that haul railway carriages and old siege machines like rams both bear the name.
